English Civil War. From sixteen forty-two to sixteen fifty-one, England was torn apart by conflict between Charles I's royalist forces and parliamentary armies. The war resulted in the king's execution, the abolition of the monarchy, and the establishment of a military dictatorship under Oliver Cromwell, fundamentally transforming England's political system and establishing principles of parliamentary sovereignty that shaped modern Britain.

The roots of the conflict lay in Charles I's religious policies. He attempted to impose Anglican practices on Scotland, provoking rebellion. He then dissolved Parliament and ruled without it from sixteen twenty-nine to sixteen forty, finally recalling Parliament in desperation over finances. When conflicts between Crown and Commons escalated into warfare, the nation split. Royalists, including aristocrats and Anglicans, fought for the Crown. Parliamentarians, called roundheads and led by Oliver Cromwell, fought for parliamentary supremacy and increasingly for religious reform and popular representation.

Cromwell's New Model Army, formed in sixteen forty-five, was revolutionary. It was a professional, disciplined force organized on meritocratic lines, with officers promoted by ability rather than birth. Their victories at Naseby in sixteen forty-five and subsequent campaigns crushed royalist resistance. But military victory led to political tensions. Parliament divided between moderates who wanted to negotiate with Charles and radicals who wanted to restructure government. Cromwell's army purged Parliament in sixteen forty-eight and put Charles I on trial for treason. In January sixteen forty-nine, he was executed, a shocking act that horrified European monarchies and demonstrated that parliamentary and popular forces had overcome divine-right absolutism in England.

What followed was the Commonwealth and Protectorate, lasting from sixteen forty-nine to sixteen sixty, characterized by Cromwell's military dictatorship, religious reformation, and colonial expansion. After Cromwell's death, the monarchy was restored in sixteen sixty under Charles II, but Parliament's authority was permanently established.
